title: How Often Should You Report Customer Feedback Insights, and How Do You Time Them to Decisions?
summary: Report feedback insights on three rhythms set by decisions: a monthly view, a brief before each planning cycle, and a note when something shifts.
body_markdown:
The quarterly feedback readout lands on a Tuesday. Product set its roadmap the Friday before. Operations made its staffing call at last week's review. The findings are accurate, well presented and too late to change anything. That's the most common way feedback reporting fails, and a more frequent report won't fix it.


Report customer feedback insights on three rhythms. Set them by the decisions they feed, not by the survey calendar. Keep a standing monthly view that each team can check on its own. Send a short brief one to two weeks before each planning cycle that the feedback should shape. Send a short note between those dates only when something shifts beyond normal variation. Thematic supports all three. Dashboards compare periods for the standing view. The Score Change waterfall explains what moved for the brief. Spike Detection workflows flag themes that move more than two standard deviations from their recent average.


Below are the five steps to set it up, a table of rhythms by team, and the mistakes that most often break it.


## The five-step process


1. **Map the decision calendar.** List every recurring decision the feedback should influence, with its date and owner.
2. **Work back to a delivery date.** Set when each insight has to arrive for the decision owner to use it.
3. **Keep a standing monthly view.** Give each team a view of its themes and score that updates without a request.
4. **Send a brief before each planning cycle.** Package what changed since the last cycle, timed to land before the decision.
5. **Send a short note when something shifts.** Report between cycles only when a theme moves beyond normal variation.


## Step 1: Map the decision calendar


Start with the decisions, not the data. Ask each team that consumes feedback three questions. Which recurring decisions does it make? When does it make them? Who makes the call?


Most organizations run on a small set of fixed clocks:


- **Annual planning and budget** , usually once a year, with a strategy offsite before it.
- **Quarterly goals and roadmap planning.** Google, for example, sets annual and quarterly objectives and key results (OKRs) and meets quarterly to grade them, according to its[re:Work guide](https://rework.withgoogle.com/en/guides/set-goals-with-okrs) .
- **Monthly business and leadership reviews.**
- **Weekly operations reviews** for contact centers, stores and service teams.
- **Account renewals and quarterly business reviews** for B2B teams.


Write these down with real dates for the next two quarters. This calendar, not the survey schedule, sets your reporting rhythm.


**Common mistake:** inheriting the cadence from the survey. A quarterly survey doesn't mean a quarterly report is useful. Forrester's 2025 feedback management research found teams are not effective at "aligning the timing of reports with key stakeholders' decision-making cadences," and that only 27%[communicate insights in a timely way](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/feedback-and-cx-measurement-programs-must-boost-their-impact-according-to-forresters-2025-survey/) .


## Step 2: Work back to a delivery date


A decision has a deadline for inputs, and it's earlier than the meeting. Product managers draft priorities before roadmap planning. Finance locks numbers before the budget review. If feedback arrives on the day of the meeting, it competes with a plan that's already written.


For each decision on the calendar, set a delivery date one to two weeks before the decision itself. That gives the owner time to read it, question it and change the plan. For weekly operations reviews, the "brief" is simply the current view, checked the day before.


**Common mistake:** timing reports to when the analysis is finished. Finish the analysis to meet the delivery date instead.


## Step 3: Keep a standing monthly view


The standing view answers "what are customers saying right now?" without anyone having to ask. It should show each team its own themes, the score those themes affect, and the change from last month.


Monthly suits most teams because it lines up with the monthly business reviews most organizations already hold. Teams that act faster can check it more often. One North American intercity bus operator used to compile survey results by hand, and found they were three to four weeks old by the time they reached the business. After moving to Thematic, station managers checked their dashboards once or twice a week, while corporate managers reviewed the month's score and themes.


In Thematic, the same dashboard can be compared by week, month, quarter or rolling 90 days, and two exact periods can be set side by side. Dashboards can be emailed on a scheduled cadence as new data loads, and Viewer seats let non-analysts see them. The guide on[automating customer feedback reporting](https://getthematic.com/insights/automate-customer-feedback-reporting) covers the setup in detail.


**Common mistake:** treating the standing view as a report to present. It's a reference. Nobody should need a meeting to read it.


## Step 4: Send a brief before each planning cycle


The pre-planning brief is the report that changes decisions. It should be short: what moved since the last cycle, why it moved, what it's worth, and what the team should consider for the plan.


Build it around the score change, not the theme list. Thematic's Score Change waterfall shows which themes pushed a score like[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) up (in green) or down (in red) between two periods, and the contributions add up to the total change. That turns "here is what customers said this quarter" into "these themes pulled the score down, and this one is growing."


Tailor the brief to the decision it feeds. For a roadmap cycle, rank themes by impact, as described in[how to prioritize your product roadmap from customer feedback](https://getthematic.com/insights/prioritize-product-roadmap-customer-feedback) . For an executive or board review, open with the decision and size it in a metric executives own, as covered in[how to report customer feedback findings to your executive team](https://getthematic.com/insights/report-customer-feedback-findings-executive-team) .


**Common mistake:** sending the brief to everyone. Send it to the people who own the decision, with a named owner for each recommended action. The article on[getting teams to act on customer feedback insights](https://getthematic.com/insights/act-on-feedback-insights-across-teams) covers ownership.


## Step 5: Send a short note when something shifts


Some changes can't wait for the next cycle. A new issue after a release, or a sharp rise in complaints about one location, needs to[reach the owner](https://getthematic.com/insights/automated-customer-insights-routing) within days.


Set a clear threshold so this doesn't turn into noise. A useful rule is to report a shift only when it falls outside a theme's normal variation. Thematic's Spike Detection workflow does this. It flags themes that move more than two standard deviations above or below their recent average, and sends the alert by email or Slack on a daily, weekly or monthly schedule. Before writing the note, check whether the change is[a real trend or a seasonal pattern](https://getthematic.com/insights/real-trend-or-seasonal-customer-feedback) .


Keep the note to three lines: what moved, how far, and who should look at it.


**Common mistake:** sending a note for every movement. If teams get a shift note every week, they stop reading them.


## What rhythm suits each team?


Team Decision it feeds Standing view Pre-planning brief Shift note


Product Quarterly roadmap planning Monthly One to two weeks before planning New issue after a release


Operations Weekly operations review Weekly Before quarterly staffing and process reviews Spike at a site or channel


Account management Renewals and quarterly business reviews Monthly, by account Before each renewal or business review Sharp drop for a key account


Executive team Annual plan and quarterly reviews Monthly summary Before each quarterly and annual review Only shifts that affect a company metric


Some programs run slower than this. Community Health System, a healthcare network, used Thematic to analyze employee engagement survey comments, and planned a twice-yearly reporting cadence that matches when survey results come in. In one three-day sprint, it produced[250 one-page department reports](https://getthematic.com/insights/community-health-systems-actionable-insights) . The rhythm should follow the decision and the data, whichever is slower.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Setting cadence by the survey calendar.** Set it by the decisions the feedback should change.
- **Delivering on the day of the meeting.** Deliver one to two weeks before, so the owner can change the plan.
- **One report for every audience.** Each team needs its own view and its own brief.
- **Reporting the score without the reasons.** Show which themes moved the score, not only that it moved.
- **Alerting on every change.** Report between cycles only when a theme moves beyond normal variation.
- **Never revisiting the calendar.** Planning dates change. Recheck the decision calendar every quarter.


## In short: how often to report customer feedback insights


Report customer feedback insights on three rhythms, set by the decisions they feed. Keep a standing monthly view for every team. Send a brief one to two weeks before each planning cycle. Send a short note between cycles only when a theme moves beyond normal variation. Thematic supports each rhythm with period-comparison dashboards, the Score Change waterfall and Spike Detection workflows, so feedback reaches the people who decide before they decide.
